title: New Orleans ship collision: What we know | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

With the wreckage of a riverboat lying on its side in the Mississippi River and a lawsuit already filed by the Port Authority of New Orleans against the owners of the tanker that hit it on Friday, federal investigators are working to learn what could have caused things to go wrong in a matter of minutes.

The focus, according to National Transportation Safety Board officials, is the tanker suddenly losing control of its steering when the rudder froze, pushing the ship into the riverbank. Investigators have listened to recordings from the ship to understand what happened in the moments leading up to the collision and said crew interviews would begin Monday.

Of the 190 people on board the riverboat, all survived, with 32 taken to the hospital. Four remained there Monday morning, with one in serious condition and three in stable condition,according to the city of New Orleans.

Here is what we know.

The NTSB’s probe will include preserving evidence from both ships and interviews with passengers and crew members.

NTSB officials said their investigation is ongoing but it is not criminal in nature.

The steering failure caused the rudder to remain completely to starboard, according to Bart Barnum, NTSB investigator in charge and senior marine accident investigator.

NTSB Member John DeLeeuw told reporters Sunday investigators will be looking at personnel and the ships involved as well as “the environment at the time.”

“I also want to mention that we don’t just investigate the things that went wrong,” DeLeeuw said. “We are also going to investigate the things that went right. There were a number of reasons of why there were no fatalities, and so we are going to take that as part of our investigation.”

The passenger riverboat had 140 passengers and 50 crew and was docked at the Thalia Street Wharf, DeLeeuw said. The tank vessel had 19 crew members and one local pilot who were headed to an oil facility upriver in Reserve, Louisiana.

Melanie Burnham, a captain for the US Coast Guard, told CNN on Monday the federal agency was “actively working to remove hazardous material” from the cruise ship.

There are 16,000 gallons of diesel fuel still aboard the ship, according to the Coast Guard.

The Port of New Orleans filed a lawsuit against the tanker owners hours after the crash.

The lawsuit, which named Thome Ship Management in Singapore and the vessel’s listed owner, Nave Shipping, said the tanker caused more than $1 million in damages to a New Orleans terminal.

The docked riverboat was struck “as a result of the negligence, gross negligence, fault or carelessness” of the tanker, Nave Shipping and Thome Ship Management, according to the lawsuit.

Four cruise ship crew members separately filed a lawsuit against the tanker owners on Saturday. The lawsuit said the collision sent the plaintiffs and others overboard and into the water, where they didn’t know “if they were going to live or die.”

The lawsuit also accused Thome Ship Management and Nave Shipping of “fault, negligence, carelessness, and omission of duty.”

Hugh Lambert, an attorney representing the four crew members named in the suit, told CNN he is seeking monetary damages for the “physical and psychological injuries” his clients suffered in the collision.

Lambert said the extent of their physical injuries has yet to be determined, but they were evaluated by first responders after the crash. The crew members, he said, likely won’t want to work on a cruise ship again.

“They thought they were going to die and drown,” Lambert said. “These kinds of things are traumatic.”

Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry hailed it as a “miracle on the Mississippi,” asall passengers made it to safety.

The cruise ship capsized within 22 minutes of the collision, prompting an emergency response to get everyone off the ship and out of the river.

About 80 people were evacuated from the boat before it capsized, said New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll.

Video from the collision’s aftermath showed at least a dozen people in life jackets being pulled from the water as other passengers climbed over the railings of the ship lying on its side.

“There had to be some kind of divine, godly intervention for this outcome,” Mayor Helena Moreno said Saturday.

CNN’s Taylor Romine, Martin Goillandeau, Isa Mudannayake, Eduardo Cuevas and Ray Sanchez contributed to this report.
